title: {{NAME}} and the Rescue Team at the End of Time
moral: The best rescue missions use every skill available, no matter how unexpected.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a bright orange rescue jacket, dark blue trousers, and heavy-duty boots — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
The temporal disturbance hit at eight in the morning.

When it cleared, the town park contained: twelve confused rabbits, four startled deer, one very alarmed fox, and a young Iguanodon who looked as though being displaced by sixty million years was not how she had planned her morning.

{{NAME}} had been testing his rescue robot, ROVER, in the park at the time.

Rover beeped.

"I see it," said {{NAME}}. "Rover, run assessment."

pages.content:
Assessment: the Iguanodon was confused, frightened, and hungry. The park animals were frightened of the Iguanodon. The temporal disturbance had created a window that would close in six hours.

Rover's solution: establish safe zones. Rover projected gentle coloured light corridors to guide the small animals away from the Iguanodon's space. The animals, surprisingly, followed the light.

{{NAME}} approached the Iguanodon with food from a park maintenance shed: a wheelbarrow full of fresh-cut grass and tree branches.

The Iguanodon looked at the wheelbarrow. Looked at him. Ate everything.

pages.content:
The challenge: getting the Iguanodon back through the temporal window before it closed.

Rover calculated the window's location (northeast corner, near the old oak) and its remaining open time (four hours and declining).

But the Iguanodon didn't want to go near the oak. She had learned, in twenty minutes, that the fox lived under it.

{{NAME}} moved the fox first, then had Rover project a path of light from the Iguanodon to the window, wide and clear and gentle.

The Iguanodon followed it slowly, sniffing at intervals.

pages.content:
At the oak, she stopped and looked back.

{{NAME}} stood thirty metres behind her. Rover beeped softly beside him.

The Iguanodon made a sound like a large cello note, low and round.

Rover translated: "Uncertain. Possible query."

"It's all right," {{NAME}} said, louder than necessary since she almost certainly didn't understand the words. "Your world is still there. It's waiting."

She looked at him for a long moment.

Then she walked through the window and was gone.

pages.content:
The window closed with a sound like a very large door settling.

The animals gradually came back to the park: rabbits first, then the deer, then the fox who inspected the area under the oak with professional thoroughness.

{{NAME}} sat on a bench with Rover beside him as the park returned to normal.

"Good job today," he told Rover.

Rover beeped twice.

That night, {{NAME}} lay in bed thinking about the Iguanodon's backward look at the window, and the cello sound, and Rover's uncertain translation, and he thought: I understood her anyway.

He fell asleep smiling.
